Area Forecast Discussion...UPDATED
National Weather Service Portland OR
355 PM PST Wed Nov 18 2026

...Updated aviation discussion...

.SYNOPSIS...A short period of mostly dry weather is expected
Thursday and Friday as a ridge moves over the region. The next
chance for rain comes on Saturday as another low pressure system
moves through. Rainfall amounts are not expected to be
impactful. Light snow will also be possible in the Cascades and
down to pass level. Conditions remain active heading into next
week but exact impacts are unclear though there is a 5-10% for a
strong system to bring impacts during the Tuesday-Thursday
timeframe.

&&

.DISCUSSION...Now through Wednesday...Scattered showers will 
continue to dissipate through the evening as a surface low well
offshore moves towards California. Conditions trend drier on 
Thursday and Friday as shortwave ridging moves over the PacNW. 
Heading into the weekend, another cold front is expected to 
impact the region, bringing light rain and light mountain snow. 
Heading into early next week, active weather is expected to 
continue with several systems moving over the region with a low 
chance for a strong, more impactful system during the middle of 
the week. 

Shifting into the details of the upcoming weather pattern. Rain and 
snow showers taper off heading into the evening and overnight hours 
along with cloud cover thinning over the area. Areas of fog will be 
possible as temperatures drop into the 30s where the ground will be 
wet. The most likely places for fog development is across the 
lowlands along the I-5 corridor through southwest Washington, 
through the Portland metro, and throughout the Willamette Valley 
after 10 PM. IF/where fog develops, it is expected to dissipate 
between 9-11 AM Thursday. Cool and dry conditions expected Thursday 
with highs in the mid to upper 40s inland and low 50s along the 
coast. Thursday night into Friday will see another potential round 
of fog as overnight lows cool into the 30s with light winds. 

The next chance for rain is expected to come on Saturday as a trough 
over the Gulf of Alaska digs southeast toward the PacNW. Timing and 
location of the cold front still show some spread among the 
ensembles. The most likely timing for the front to reach the coast 
is between 7 AM and noon and spreading inland by the afternoon. 
Rainfall totals are expected to be on the lighter side with chances 
for 48 hour totals to exceed 0.50 inches Saturday through Monday 
varying across the forecast area. The best chances are along the 
coast at 50-60%, 30-40% over the coast range and 10-30% across the 
interior lowlands. There is also a chance for snow in the Cascades 
as snow levels drop to 2000-3500 feet Saturday evening. 
Accumulations over 48 hours are expected to be light with a 40-60% 
for 2 inches at pass level, higher chances above 5000 feet. Travel 
conditions could become hazardous at times. 

Active weather is expected to continue into next week, exactly how 
impactful is still unclear given model spread. Another digging 
trough is expected to move toward the PacNW during the Tuesday 
through Thursday timeframe. A majority of models have a very strong 
low developing offshore which would lead to lesser impacts across 
Oregon and Washington. A small fraction, about 5-10% of members have 
the low developing closer to the coast which could bring stronger, 
damaging winds to the forecast area. Another scenario is the main 
low developing well offshore but a secondary meso-low developing 
along the cold front which could impact the coast. With a decent 
amount of spread in the main low development and possibly a 
secondary low, the overall certainty of a major storm is low but not 
zero. Details should become clearer in the next few days as models 
continue to adjust. -19

&&

.AVIATION...Through 18Z Thursday...Radar imagery and terminal
observations as of mid Wednesday afternoon depicts scattered rain 
showers across northwest Oregon and southwest Washington as a low 
pressure system moves through the area. This system will gradually 
move northward this evening, decreasing showers and returning 
predominately VFR conditions. Satellite imagery is also showing 
increased clearing behind this system. Clear skies, calm winds, and 
a moist ground will be favorable for fog development tonight across 
the Willamette Valley. An exception would be the eastern Portland 
Metro Area like KPDX and KTTD as easterly winds may prevent fog 
development. Overnight lows will also fall into the low to mid 30s 
early Thursday morning, so there may also be some frost development 
over metal surfaces. The biggest uncertainty is whether or not 
Valley terminals see fog or frost. If a terminal frosts out, there 
may not be fog development. After 18-20z Thu, any fog or low clouds 
that develop overnight should begin to dissipate. However, given 
this time of year with low sun angle, wouldn't be surprised if some 
locations fail to clear out. Winds generally light and variable. 

KPDX AND APPROACHES...Predominately VFR conditions through this 
evening with light scattered showers. Easterly winds gradually 
weaken to around 5 kt or less overnight. There is a 20-30% chance 
for fog development at any given hour between 12-18z Thu, however, 
if easterly winds persist then this can prevent fog.     -10 

&&

.MARINE...A low pressure system moving through the waters is
bringing south-southwesterly winds to the waters south of Cape
Falcon and east-southeasterly winds from Cape Falcon northward.
Winds have fallen below 15 kt and are expected to remain weak
through the end of the week. Seas also remain around 10-14 ft at
13-14 seconds as a westerly swell persists. Small Craft Advisories
remain in effect for the inner waters out to 10 NM through 10 AM
Thursday, while Hazardous Seas Warnings remain in effect for the
outer waters beyond 10 NM offshore through 10 PM tonight.

On Thursday, winds briefly shift northerly as high pressure re- 
builds. The westerly swell will also subside, bringing seas down 
to 7-9 ft at 12-13 seconds by Thursday afternoon. Winds turn more 
southerly on Friday ahead of the next system, but gusts remain 
below 20 kt. Seas also fall to 6-7 ft by the end of the week.

The next system arrives late Friday night into Saturday, returning
breezy southerly winds and small craft wind gusts up to 30 kt.
There is also a 40-70% chance for isolated gale force wind gusts
up to 35 kt across the outer waters beyond 10-20 NM offshore. For
the inner waters and Columbia River Bar, chances for isolated gale
force wind gusts are lower around 20-30%. Seas gradually build
over the weekend as another westerly swell moves in, with high
confidence (>80%) for seas building again to 10 ft or greater.
